q: What is the difference between an ML model and an ML system?
short: The model maps inputs to predictions; the system includes UI, data collection, storage, serving, business logic, logging, monitoring and the processes that keep the model working for users.
example: Payments and user management have nothing to do with ML but are essential.
mistakes: Equating the model with the product.

q: What is hidden technical debt in ML systems?
short: The large, often untested infrastructure around a small ML core (configuration, data collection, feature extraction, verification, resource management, serving, monitoring) that accumulates maintenance cost and failure risk.
example: A config typo silently changes a feature.
follow: How do you pay it down?

q: Model-centric vs system-centric view?
short: Model-centric improves algorithms/features/hyperparameters for accuracy; system-centric improves data, infrastructure, deployment and UX for reliable real-world performance.
example: Batching transcription vs a better acoustic model.

q: What does a production ML pipeline add to a 'course' pipeline?
short: Evaluating and monitoring the model on production data, selecting production data for retraining, and updating/deploying the model regularly.
detail: Turns a line into a loop.
follow: How do you choose retraining data?

q: Give examples of ML as core vs auxiliary functionality.
short: Core: transcription service (speech recognition is the product). Auxiliary: audit-risk prediction inside tax software.
detail: Affects how much effort and risk ML carries.
example: Spam filter in an email product is auxiliary but high-volume.
follow: How does this change fallback design?

q: Predictive vs generative vs agentic AI?
short: Predictive forecasts from past data; generative creates content from instructions using foundation models; agentic pursues goals autonomously by reasoning, planning, using tools and iterating.
detail: Agentic = GenAI + reasoning + tools + feedback loops.
example: Churn score; product description; trip booking.

q: What is systems thinking in ML engineering?
short: Understanding the system's goals and environment, designing and integrating ML with non-ML components, and coordinating many roles and stakeholders, including planning for ML mistakes.
follow: Example of an ML error harming users?

q: What did the transcription start-up case teach?
short: Research success doesn't equal product success: noisy data, latency, compute cost, product ecosystem, fragile pipelines, team gaps and fairness all require engineering beyond ML.
example: Live captions need near real-time inference.

q: Name the nine stages of the ML workflow.
short: Model requirements, data collection, data cleaning, data labelling, feature engineering, model training, model evaluation, deployment, monitoring, with feedback loops.
example: Evaluation sends you back to collection.
follow: Which stage is implicit in CNNs?

q: What does cloud-native mean for ML workloads?
short: Running ML on containers, microservices, service meshes, immutable infrastructure and declarative APIs, typically orchestrated by Kubernetes on public, private or hybrid clouds.
follow: Which layer do data scientists own?

q: Your ML component will sometimes be wrong. How do you design the system around it?
short: Quantify error costs, use calibrated confidences and thresholds, route low-confidence cases to humans or rules, add guardrails and undo, show uncertainty in UX, monitor errors by slice, and plan fallbacks when the model is unavailable.
follow: How do you choose the threshold?

q: Why must production pipelines select data for retraining rather than use everything?
short: Old data reflects outdated patterns; recency-weighted or windowed data adapts to drift, and selection can target slices where the model fails. But windows must be large enough to avoid noise and forgetting.

q: Compute costs exceed revenue in the transcription start-up. What would you change?
short: Batch non-urgent jobs, cache and reuse, smaller/quantised models for most traffic with escalation to large ones, spot instances, autoscaling to zero, measure cost per minute per tier, price by latency tier.
mistakes: Optimising cost without accuracy checks per slice.

q: How do the EDDA and SE tracks interact?
short: EDDA asks whether ML is suitable, sets model requirements and iterates on data/models; SE does requirements, design, implementation, system test and operation. They meet at design (model requirements), integration and operation.

q: Why does generative AI need different infrastructure than predictive AI?
short: Much higher compute (specialised accelerators), massive diverse data, complex training, highly elastic scaling, high-throughput low-latency storage, and high-bandwidth networking for distributed training, vs moderate, general-purpose, batch-friendly needs for predictive models.
example: GPU clusters vs CPU batch jobs.

q: What engineering lessons come from the 28-model driving system?
short: Models feed each other, so errors propagate; code does critical pre/post-processing, validation and decisions; multi-sensor fusion and scenario-based model selection add complexity; test coverage is low and system-level QA is essential.
example: Lane detector failure affects prediction and planning.

q: Which SE practices were adapted for ML in large software teams?
short: Agile/DevOps integration, end-to-end pipelines, data engineering as core, experimentation-driven development, versioning of models and data, continuous evaluation and monitoring, model debugging/interpretability, cross-functional teams, system-level testing, process maturity models.

q: Sketch a monitoring-triggered retraining loop.
short: for each period: score live batch with delayed labels; if metric < threshold: build training window from recent data; retrain; evaluate vs current on a holdout; promote if better; log versions.

q: How do you reduce hidden technical debt in an ML system?
short: Treat glue as product code: data validation and contracts, feature stores to remove training-serving skew, config as versioned code with tests, pipeline orchestration with lineage, removal of dead features and experimental paths, monitoring with ownership, and architectural boundaries between components.

q: Design the system for a medical transcription product where some errors are critical.
short: Domain-specific evaluation sets and per-dialect slices, confidence-based highlighting, mandatory human review for medication/dose terms, audit logs, versioned models with rollback, latency tiers, privacy (PHI) controls, and monitoring of critical-term error rates.
follow: How do you measure critical errors?

q: What changes when a system has many interacting ML components?
short: Entanglement (change one, change all), cascading errors, hidden feedback loops, versioning of interfaces between models, integration testing across components, scenario-based selection logic, and system-level metrics rather than per-model metrics.
example: Detector retrain shifts downstream tracker inputs.
follow: How do you version model interfaces?
mistakes: Retraining one model without re-validating consumers.

q: When is agentic AI the wrong choice?
short: When a deterministic workflow or predictive model suffices, when errors are costly and actions irreversible, when latency/cost budgets are tight, or when tool permissions and audit can't be controlled; prefer constrained workflows with human approval.

q: How would you assess an ML team's process maturity?
short: Look at automation (pipelines, CI/CD for data and models), reproducibility (versioning, lineage), evaluation rigour (holdouts, slices, human review), monitoring and incident response, cross-functional collaboration, and continuous improvement, on a CMM-like scale from ad hoc to optimised.
follow: What is the first step up?

q: Live accuracy is falling slowly but steadily. How do you decide between retraining and redesign?
short: Diagnose drift type (covariate vs concept), check data pipeline changes, evaluate retraining on recent windows; if retrained models also decay fast or features lost meaning, redesign features, add online learning or change the decision process.
detail: Ex1 shows retraining recovers accuracy under gradual drift.
